says: A support definition already visited earlier in the same check counts as not met, even if it was met then and is not part of a circular reference. For an All-of definition, a shared sub-definition reached from two places therefore fails the whole definition the second time.

A plain supported-on product entry is met when the computer lists that product, or, for a parent product, when it lists any sub-product (or a sub-product's child). A version-range entry is met only by a sub-product, or its child, whose version lies within the range, minimum 0 and maximum the highest known version by default; listing the parent itself does not meet it. A product with no sub-products is met only by being listed. An entry with no known product is met only when unknown entries are approved.

A support definition is combined as All-of only when the caller opts in to honouring All-of and the definition is marked All-of; otherwise every definition is treated as any-one-of. An All-of definition is met when every entry is met, so one with no entries is met. An any-one-of definition is met when any entry is met, so one with no entries is not met. Products are checked before nested definitions.

When an Enabled policy has a text-list element that does not keep other values, the element's key is cleared first. With a list supplied, items are then saved under names the person chose, or numbered 1, 2, 3 after the element's name prefix when it has one, else under the item text itself. With no list supplied, the key is left cleared when the element does not keep others, and untouched when it does.
When an Enabled policy has a drop-down element, the chosen item's value is written and then the item's value list; both go under the element's key unless the item or its list names another key.
When an Enabled policy has a multi-line text element, the text is saved as a multi-string value.

Every on-value, off-value and value list written for a policy, a checkbox or a drop-down item (for Enabled and Disabled alike) follows one scheme. A list item uses its own registry key when it names one, else the list's default key, else the key of the policy or element that owns the list. A value marked delete is deleted, a number is saved as DWORD and text as a string; an absent value writes nothing.

Clearing a key in a POL file forgets the stored record of every value in it, so those values no longer hold data. The clearing marker it leaves makes every value in that key count as Queued for deletion, until a real value is set for it; they do not read as Not configured.

Applying a policy state to a SPOL script policy fails before anything else when the policy ID is unknown. Otherwise the comment is saved only when comments are available and the script's comment is not empty; an empty comment never erases an existing one. Any earlier state of the policy is then forgotten, so Not Configured is reached by that forgetting alone. If writing the new state then fails, the policy stays forgotten and its earlier state is lost.

Writing a policy state to a source decides only Enabled and Disabled. Not Configured and Unknown write nothing, so a caller must forget the policy's earlier values first for Not Configured to result. Enabled and Disabled writes do not remove stale values left by a previous state, apart from the deletes and clears the elements themselves make.

A REG file is only a write target. Setting a value, deleting a value, clearing a key and forgetting a key clearance work. Reading a value, checking a value, checking queued deletion, listing value names and forgetting a value are not implemented and fail. A difference-apply that must forget values fails if it targets a REG file, and a REG file cannot be read back as a policy source.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when an option line under an Enabled policy has no ': ' separator. The message is the system's own, not a Policy Plus text.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when the same option name appears twice under one policy.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when an option list opened with '[' is never closed with ']' before the text ends.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when a list entry holds no quoted text, or when entries after the first hold fewer strings than the first requires.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when a policy header has no space between section and policy ID, or when the header is last in the text, or the state line is missing after it.
